segments.name: The Civil Service of Great Britain

stops.name: 83 Dwight Street, New Haven, the birth
stops.date_confidence: attested. Birth on 18 December 1888 and the Dwight Street address are documented; Moses lived here his first nine years, two blocks from Yale. FLAGGED: the research pool's coordinate plotted roughly 250 m east, nearer York and Park Streets; corrected here to Dwight Street between Chapel and Elm.
stops.campa: In a house on Dwight Street, two blocks from the Yale campus, Emanuel and Bella Moses have their second son. The family keeps a department store and property enough that neither Robert nor his older brother Paul will ever need a salary. Bella is the engine of the household: Ethical Culture, settlement work, civic committees, and a conviction that a private fortune exists to be spent in public. The Moseses belong to a New Haven of Yale men and German-Jewish merchants who do not go to synagogue. Robert lives in this house until he is nine years old.
stops.quote: On my father's side I am descended from Spanish Jews, while my mother came from Bavarian Jewish stock. My ancestors came to the United States more than 100 years ago.
stops.quote_source: Robert Moses, interview with William Reswick, The Day, 26 October 1934
suggested_refs: 83 Dwight Street, New Haven, the Moses family house until 1897
sources: NPS, Gateway National Recreation Area, biographical profile of Robert Moses
NYPL finding aid, Robert Moses papers, archives.nypl.org/mss/2071
JTA archive, William Reswick interview with Robert Moses, The Day, 26 October 1934

stops.name: East 46th Street, Manhattan, the family comes down from New Haven
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year 1897; month and day not established in the sources consulted, defaulted to 01-01. The East 46th Street address is the one from which the 1982 dedication parade for Robert Moses Playground set off, given there as 20 East 46th Street.
stops.campa: Emanuel Moses sells the New Haven store and the New Haven property and moves the household to Manhattan, where he will not work again. They land inside the reform elite: Ethical Culture, the settlement houses, the committees that investigate tenements and publish reports about them. Bella runs a Lower East Side program and gives money away by plan rather than by impulse. Robert is nine years old when they arrive, and the talk he grows up inside is of tenement law, sanitation districts, and how a city ought to be arranged.
stops.quote: Members of my family belong to the Ethical Culture group. My grandmother was one of the founders of the Ethical Culture Society and was associated with Dr. Felix Adler.
stops.quote_source: Robert Moses, interview with William Reswick, The Day, 26 October 1934
suggested_refs: The Ethical Culture Society of New York and the settlement-house milieu of Bella Moses
sources: Encyclopedia.com, Robert Moses biography
NPS, Gateway National Recreation Area, biographical profile of Robert Moses

stops.name: Yale Old Campus, New Haven, the prize scholar
stops.date_confidence: attested that Moses entered Yale at seventeen and graduated cum laude and Phi Beta Kappa in 1909, with prizes in Latin and public speaking, work on the Yale Courant and varsity water polo. Dated to the start of the 1905 academic year to open the segment; the exact matriculation day is not established.
stops.campa: He enters Yale at seventeen and does everything a scholarship boy does without needing a scholarship: prizes in Latin and in public speaking, the Yale Courant, varsity water polo. He also goes out and finds a donor to fund the swimming team himself, and when the athletic association will not take the money on his terms he resigns from the team and does not go back. The Atlantic is still telling that story about him thirty years later, by which time it has stopped sounding like an anecdote about swimming. He graduates cum laude and Phi Beta Kappa in 1909 and goes on to Oxford.
suggested_refs: The Atlantic profile of Robert Moses, February 1939, on the Yale years
sources: Columbia University C250 biographical record
The Atlantic, profile of Robert Moses, February 1939

stops.name: Wadham College, Oxford, the permanent civil service
stops.date_confidence: attested for the degrees: Wadham College, jurisprudence, B.A. 1911, M.A. 1913. FLAGGED: the widely repeated claim that Moses was elected president of the Oxford Union is NOT supported by the Columbia C250 record cited for it, nor by any source reachable in this pass, and is omitted here. An Oxford M.A. is conferred by seniority without residence, so 1913 does not place him in Oxford. Dated to the start of Michaelmas term 1909. Pin inherited as the corpus's canonical Oxford coordinate.
stops.campa: At Wadham he reads jurisprudence and finds the thing he will spend fifty years trying to build in America: a permanent civil service, entered by examination, promoted on record, insulated from patronage, run by an educated class that governs because it is qualified to. What he carries home is the premise that the best men should be handed power and then left alone with it. He takes his B.A. in 1911; the M.A. of 1913 comes by seniority and does not require him to be in England to collect it. Whether he ever spoke at the Union, as the profiles keep saying he did, is not in any record reached here.
suggested_refs: Wadham College, Oxford, jurisprudence, 1909-1911
sources: Columbia University C250 biographical record

stops.name: 261 Broadway, Manhattan, the Bureau of Municipal Research
stops.date_confidence: attested that Moses joined the Bureau of Municipal Research in 1913, served as technical adviser on civil-service reform under Mayor John Purroy Mitchel, and lost the post after Mitchel's defeat in November 1917; the merit plan was never implemented. Month and day of appointment not established, defaulted to 01-01. Marriage to Mary Louise Sims of Dodgeville, Wisconsin, dated August 1915. FLAGGED: the pool's coordinate matched no known Bureau address; the pin here is 261 Broadway, the Bureau's address in this period.
stops.campa: He joins the Bureau of Municipal Research and becomes technical adviser to Mayor John Purroy Mitchel's Civil Service Commission, drafting a merit system that would grade and rank every employee of the city by measured performance. The clerks hate it, the unions hate it, Tammany hates it, and it is never put into effect. In 1915 he marries Mary Louise Sims of Dodgeville, Wisconsin, whom he met in the reform offices. Mitchel is beaten in November 1917 and Moses goes out of the building with him. He is twenty-nine and unemployed.
suggested_refs: The New York Bureau of Municipal Research at 261 Broadway and the Mitchel civil-service reform papers
sources: Columbia University C250 biographical record

stops.name: Columbia University, Morningside Heights, the doctorate
stops.date_confidence: attested; Ph.D. in political science, Columbia, 1914, the dissertation published as The Civil Service of Great Britain by Columbia University Press. Month defaulted to the June commencement; the exact conferral date is not established in the sources consulted.
stops.campa: The doctorate is taken in political science while he is already at work downtown, and the dissertation is published as The Civil Service of Great Britain. The English service he describes is entered by open examination, graded, and shielded by tenure from whichever party holds the government. Against it he sets the American spoils system, with contempt and at length: the machine, the trade, the appointment made for the appointer's reasons. He is twenty-five and has held no office of any consequence. Columbia University Press prints the book in 1914.
suggested_refs: Robert Moses, The Civil Service of Great Britain (Columbia University Press, 1914)
sources: Columbia University C250 biographical record

stops.name: New York State Capitol, Albany, the Reconstruction Commission
stops.date_confidence: attested; Moses joined the New York State Reconstruction Commission as chief of staff under Belle Moskowitz in 1919, following Alfred E. Smith's election as governor, and drafted a plan consolidating roughly 187 state agencies. Month and day not established, defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: Belle Moskowitz, who runs Governor Al Smith's brain trust, hires the unemployed reformer as chief of staff of the New York State Reconstruction Commission. His assignment is to redraw the state government itself, and he proposes folding some hundred and eighty-seven agencies into a cabinet answering to the governor. From Smith he learns the two things Oxford could not teach, how a bill is written and how an appropriation is hidden inside one. Smith left school at fourteen for the Fulton Fish Market. He reads every draft Moses hands him and understands every line of it.
suggested_refs: The 1919 report of the New York State Reconstruction Commission
sources: Columbia University C250 biographical record
Robert A. Caro, 'The Best Bill Drafter in Albany', The New Yorker, 22 July 1974

stops.name: Belmont Lake State Park, North Babylon, the two commissions
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1924 for both appointments, president of the Long Island State Park Commission and chairman of the New York State Council of Parks, held for roughly forty years. The exact appointment date is not established in the sources consulted; month defaulted to April to order the segment.
stops.campa: Smith makes him president of the Long Island State Park Commission and chairman of the State Council of Parks, and Moses has written his own enabling statute. Buried in it is appropriation: the commission may take land by entering it and posting notice, leaving the owner to sue afterward for what it was worth. He will hold these two posts for about forty years. From a headquarters in the woods at Belmont Lake he begins assembling Jones Beach, Sunken Meadow, Heckscher and Bethpage, parkway by parkway, farm by farm.
suggested_refs: The 1924 Long Island State Park Commission enabling act and its appropriation clause
sources: Columbia University C250 biographical record

stops.name: Northern State Parkway, near Roslyn, the road bent around the estates
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction [R]. The realignment of the Northern State Parkway away from the large north-shore estates, including Otto Kahn's golf course, is documented in Caro's The Power Broker (1974); the imputation of personal payments is disputed by later scholars, who contest the bribe reading and not the route. Dated 1925 to sit inside the 1924-1927 negotiations; no single day applies. The quote is [R]: no authenticated first utterance has been located.
stops.campa: The parkway to the beaches has to cross the north shore estates, and the estates fight. Otto Kahn's golf course, the Whitney land, the Winthrop land: their owners organize, retain counsel, and contribute to the survey costs. The road moves. It moves south onto the potato farms of smaller men who have no counsel and no committee, and the farmers stand at their fences watching surveyors drive stakes through crops they planted in the spring. Caro reads the episode as the first lesson learned. Later scholars dispute the payment and not the route.
stops.quote: If the end doesn't justify the means, what does?
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Robert Moses; used by Robert A. Caro as the title of his New Yorker excerpt, 29 July 1974, and quoted in The Power Broker. No authenticated first utterance located.
suggested_refs: Caro, The Power Broker (1974), on the Northern State Parkway realignment; later scholarly rebuttals of the bribe account
sources: Robert A. Caro, The Power Broker (1974)
Later scholarly commentary disputing the personal-bribe reading, summarized in the research dossier

stops.name: Albany, Executive Chamber, Roosevelt declines to reappoint him
stops.date_confidence: attested; Moses became New York secretary of state under Governor Smith on 17 January 1927 and left the post on 1 January 1929 when the incoming governor, Franklin D. Roosevelt, declined to reappoint him. Dated to the day the office lapsed. Pin inherited from the interlock pass as the Albany Executive Chamber coordinate.
stops.campa: Smith has made him secretary of state of New York, cabinet rank held alongside the park authorities, and Moses has used the office to run the state's parks as a private department. Then Smith loses the presidency, Franklin Roosevelt takes Albany, and one of the new governor's first acts is to decline the reappointment. The two have already learned to dislike each other: Roosevelt the patrician who wants the credit, Moses the technician who wants the money. The feud will run the length of the New Deal. Moses keeps the parks.
suggested_refs: The Moses-Roosevelt correspondence in the NYPL Robert Moses papers
sources: NYPL finding aid, Robert Moses papers, archives.nypl.org/mss/2071

stops.name: Jones Beach State Park, Long Island, the opening
stops.date_confidence: attested for the opening, 4 August 1929, and for the park's design and construction under Moses. The low-bridges intention is [R]: Caro's The Power Broker (1974) reports it from testimony by Moses's aide Sidney Shapiro, later scholars treat it as unproven, and no written order has been located. The physical clearances are not disputed; the motive is.
stops.campa: Six miles of ocean beach on a barrier island that was sand and marsh grass five years ago, and the state has put on it two bathhouses in Ozark sandstone and Barbizon brick, a water tower raised as a Venetian campanile, boardwalks, mooring basins, attendants in white who are forbidden to take tips. No billboards. No hot dog stands. Moses designs the litter baskets himself. The parkway overpasses that bring the crowds in are low, and Caro's account holds that they were built low to keep out buses and the people who ride them.
suggested_refs: The Jones Beach water tower and the two original bathhouses, 1929

stops.name: The Arsenal, Central Park, the first unified Parks Commissioner
stops.date_confidence: attested to January 1934, when Moses became New York City's first unified Parks Commissioner after Fiorello La Guardia took office and the five borough park departments were consolidated; the exact day of taking office is not established in the sources consulted, defaulted to 01-01. Central Park was laid out to the 1858 Greensward plan of Frederick Law Olmsted and Calvert Vaux; the pin is the Arsenal, the department's headquarters.
stops.campa: La Guardia takes City Hall in a bankrupt city and hands Moses the five borough park departments welded into one, the weld being a consolidation bill Moses drafted himself. He moves into the Arsenal at Sixty-Fourth Street and inherits Central Park, laid out by Frederick Law Olmsted and Calvert Vaux seventy-six years earlier and by now gone to seed. Within a year he has relief labour inside it by the thousand, rebuilding the zoo and the Tavern on the Green and putting playgrounds at the entrances. The Greensward plan had specified no playgrounds anywhere in the park.

stops.name: Albany, the only election he ever contests
stops.date_confidence: attested; Moses ran as the Republican nominee for governor of New York on 6 November 1934 against the Democratic incumbent Herbert H. Lehman and lost by roughly 800,000 votes, about 36.7 per cent to 58 per cent. The interview quoted was published in The Day on 26 October 1934, during the campaign.
stops.campa: The Republicans nominate him for governor against Herbert Lehman, and he runs the only campaign of his life. He is a disastrous candidate. He insults the electorate, attacks Lehman personally, is attacked in his turn over his ancestry, and answers the ancestry question in a Yiddish daily without a word of apology. He loses by about eight hundred thousand votes, 36.7 per cent of the ballot against Lehman's 58. He goes back to the Arsenal and to Belmont Lake, and he never stands for election again.
stops.quote: I have never denied my Jewish descent.
stops.quote_source: Robert Moses, interview with William Reswick, The Day, 26 October 1934
suggested_refs: The Day, 26 October 1934, William Reswick's campaign interview with Moses
sources: JTA archive report of the Reswick interview, The Day, 26 October 1934

stops.name: Astoria Play Center, Queens, eleven pools in one summer
stops.date_confidence: attested; eleven monumental public swimming pools opened across the five boroughs in the summer of 1936, built under the Parks Department with WPA and PWA labour. The pin is the Astoria Play Center, standing for the group; the exact opening day of the Astoria pool is not established in the sources consulted, and individual openings ran through that summer.
stops.campa: Eleven swimming pools open across the five boroughs in a single season, put up with federal relief labour in a common vocabulary of brick, cast concrete and iron, each sized for thousands of bathers and floodlit for swimming at night. The Astoria pool holds Olympic trials the summer it opens. Children who have never been in water deeper than a hydrant spray learn to swim in these pools, in neighbourhoods that had no public bath at all. The openings run right through the summer of 1936, one pool after another.
suggested_refs: The eleven WPA pools of 1936: Astoria, McCarren, Hamilton Fish, Crotona, Sunset Park and the rest
sources: NYC Parks, official history of the pools, nycgovparks.org/about/history/pools

stops.name: Triborough Bridge, Randall's Island, the authority opens its bridge
stops.date_confidence: attested; the Triborough Bridge opened 11 July 1936, with federal Public Works Administration participation reported at $44.2 million. Moses had reshaped the stalled Triborough Bridge Authority and become its chairman in 1934.
stops.campa: Three bridges and their approach roads meeting on Randall's Island, stalled since the crash, finished with about forty-four million federal dollars, open to traffic. What matters is not the steel. It is the Triborough Bridge and Tunnel Authority: a public corporation with its own bonds, its own police force, its own revenue, and a chairman no mayor can remove. Every car that crosses pays a toll, the toll pays the bondholders, and whatever is left over stays inside the Authority, where no voter and no mayor can reach it. The bridge opens to traffic on 11 July 1936.
suggested_refs: The Triborough Bridge and Tunnel Authority bond covenants, the legal instrument of Moses's independence
sources: NYPL finding aid, Robert Moses papers, archives.nypl.org/mss/2071

segments.name: The Refusal, and the Method Exported

stops.name: Flushing Meadows, Queens, the ash heap made a fairground
stops.date_confidence: attested to the fair's opening, 30 April 1939. Moses's department prepared the site and the approach roads; the fair corporation was headed by Grover Whalen, not by Moses, a distinction routinely blurred in secondary accounts. The site was not finished as parkland when the fair closed in 1940.
stops.campa: The Corona ash dump, cinders tipped by the truckload for thirty years, is graded flat and turned into a fairground. Grover Whalen runs the World's Fair corporation; Moses runs the land and the roads that reach it, and the arrangement he writes returns the site to him as parkland when the gates close. The fair loses money. The park is not finished. When the gates shut in 1940 the meadow is left strewn with foundations, service roads and rubble, and it stays that way. He will be back in 1964.
suggested_refs: The 1939-40 New York World's Fair corporation records, NYPL archival collections
sources: NYPL finding aid for the 1939-40 New York World's Fair records
NYC Municipal Archives account of the Flushing Meadows fairgrounds

stops.name: Castle Clinton, Battery Park, the bridge the War Department refuses
stops.date_confidence: attested; the federal War Department rejected the proposed Brooklyn-Battery Bridge on 17 July 1939 on navigation and national-defence grounds, after opposition from preservationists including George McAneny and Albert Bard. A tunnel was built instead. Moses's subsequent campaign against Castle Clinton ran to about 1950, when most of the fort was saved.
stops.campa: He wants a bridge from the Battery to Brooklyn, six lanes on a viaduct across the harbour mouth past the old fort. Preservationists led by George McAneny and Albert Bard go over his head to Washington, and the War Department kills it: a dropped span would bottle up the Brooklyn Navy Yard. It is the first time an outside authority has simply stopped him, and he does not take it as a lesson. He builds the tunnel, closes the aquarium inside Castle Clinton, and spends the next decade trying to have the fort pulled down.
suggested_refs: Castle Clinton National Monument, saved from demolition in the 1940s campaign
sources: New York Preservation Archive Project, Brooklyn-Battery Bridge history, nypap.org
New York Preservation Archive Project, Castle Clinton preservation history

stops.name: Portland, Oregon, the method sold by the report
stops.date_confidence: attested that the report Portland Improvement was produced by Moses's organization in 1943 and is digitized by Portland State University, proposing a downtown freeway loop among roughly $60 million of works, and that Portland later built a partial loop modified by federal and local planners. Month and day of the visit and of the report's presentation are not established, defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: A Portland civic committee pays for a visit and receives Portland Improvement: a downtown freeway loop and some sixty million dollars of arterial work, bound and printed. Moses is in the city a matter of days. The document is produced by his New York staff in his New York idiom, and it reads Portland's river-and-grid downtown the way it would read the Bronx. Portland builds a partial version of the loop over the two decades following, altered by federal and local planners, and is still arguing about the pieces of it.
suggested_refs: Portland Improvement (1943), digitized at pdxscholar.library.pdx.edu/oscdl_bonner/207
sources: Portland State University digitized report, Portland Improvement, 1943

stops.name: São Paulo, the survey commissioned by Rockefeller
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction [R]. The commission by Nelson Rockefeller's International Basic Economy Corporation is recorded in the Rockefeller Archive Center collections and dated 1950; the extent of Moses's own presence in Brazil and the fate of the plan are not established in the sources consulted. Month and day defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: Nelson Rockefeller's International Basic Economy Corporation brings him to Brazil to head a survey and planning programme for São Paulo, a city taking in people faster than any other in the hemisphere. The method travels intact: count the traffic, draw the arterials, price the takings, hand over the bound report. He is sixty-one, and the New York work has become a product with a fee attached, carried by his consultants to other cities that want what New York appears to have. How long he was actually in Brazil, and what São Paulo did with the plan afterwards, is not established in any source reached here.
suggested_refs: Rockefeller Archive Center, International Basic Economy Corporation records, dimes.rockarch.org
sources: Rockefeller Archive Center record of the IBEC São Paulo programme

stops.name: City Hall, Manhattan, Construction Coordinator
stops.date_confidence: attested that the post of City Construction Coordinator was created for Moses in 1946 under Mayor William O'Dwyer, and that he sat on the City Planning Commission from 1942. FLAGGED: the NYPL finding aid prints the two start years transposed, giving Construction Coordinator 1942-1960 and Planning Commissioner 1946-1960; standard accounts reverse them, and the research pool propagated the transposition. This file follows 1942 Planning, 1946 Coordinator. Month and day not established, defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: Mayor William O'Dwyer invents an office that has never existed, City Construction Coordinator, and gives it to Moses, who has held a seat on the City Planning Commission since 1942. He is now parks commissioner, planning commissioner, construction coordinator, chairman of Triborough, chairman of the State Council of Parks, president of the Long Island State Park Commission, and chairman of the Mayor's Committee on Slum Clearance. Federal highway money and federal housing money now enter the city across a single desk, and it is his. He draws no salary from most of the offices he holds.
suggested_refs: The list of Moses's simultaneous offices, 1946-1960, in the NYPL finding aid
sources: NYPL finding aid, Robert Moses papers, archives.nypl.org/mss/2071
Wikipedia, 'Robert Moses', infobox office dates

stops.name: United Nations Headquarters, East River, the roads to the world's house
stops.date_confidence: Le Corbusier's presence on the United Nations board of design in New York in 1947, contributing the Secretariat slab scheme, is attested in his own journey file. Moses's coordinating role at the same site, covering traffic, site preparation and city-state relations after the Rockefeller family assembled the land in 1946, is reported in the research dossier and was NOT independently confirmed against a UN or Rockefeller primary source in this pass; treat that half as [R]. Dated October 1946 to the site-assembly period; no single day applies.
stops.campa: The Rockefellers buy the slaughterhouse blocks on the East River and give them to the United Nations, and the city has to make the gift work: approaches, traffic, the legislation by which state and city convey the land. Moses handles that side of it. The building belongs to a board of design under Wallace Harrison on which Le Corbusier sits and quarrels, and Le Corbusier will leave New York convinced the Secretariat was taken from him. Moses claims no part of the architecture, and his own share of the work is the half of the record that is thinnest. The drive runs under the site in a tunnel, and the delegations arrive by car.

stops.name: Cross Bronx Expressway, East Tremont, the line that does not move
stops.date_confidence: attested that construction began in stages in 1948 and continued into the 1960s. Displacement estimates of 40,000 to 60,000 along the full corridor come from the New York City Mayor's Office Cross Bronx reimagining study transcript; Caro's narrative centres on about 1,500 residents in the East Tremont section. Month and day defaulted to 01-01. The quote is verified in Caro, chapter 36, sourced there to Moses's own Public Works: A Dangerous Trade.
stops.campa: The line is drawn straight across the borough, a trench blasted for miles through rock and through whatever is standing on the rock. At East Tremont the tenants of the condemned blocks ask for a route two streets south, through a parking lot and a row of shops, and bring an engineer's drawing to show that it can be done. Moses will not move the line. Displacement along the whole corridor is put at between forty and sixty thousand people; Caro counts about fifteen hundred in the East Tremont section alone, and the two figures measure different things. The work runs in stages for sixteen years.
stops.quote: You can draw any kind of picture you like on a clean slate and indulge your every whim in the wilderness in laying out a New Delhi, Canberra or Brasilia, but when you operate in an overbuilt metropolis, you have to hack your way with a meat ax.
stops.quote_source: Robert Moses, from a speech, quoted in Robert A. Caro, The Power Broker (1974), chapter 36, sourced there to Moses's Public Works: A Dangerous Trade (1970)
suggested_refs: The East Tremont alternative alignment plan submitted by the tenants' committee
sources: New York City Mayor's Office, Cross Bronx Expressway reimagining study transcript, December 2022

stops.name: Manhattantown, Upper West Side, the write-down
stops.date_confidence: attested that the city conveyed the Manhattantown tract to a sponsor group headed by Samuel Caspert at a sharply written-down price, and that investigators later documented delays, continued rent collection in condemned buildings, and weak supervision; the Senate Banking Committee hearings are the source, as summarized by Themis Chronopoulos in the Journal of Urban History. No indictment of Moses followed. Month and day defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: Blocks of the Upper West Side are condemned under Title I and handed to a sponsor group at a written-down price, against the promise of new housing. The sponsors demolish slowly, go on collecting rent from tenants in buildings already condemned, and let the ground sit. Senate investigators take testimony on the whole arrangement. Moses is not indicted and does not resign. Why his committee kept choosing sponsors on their connections rather than on their books is a question the hearings put and never answered.
suggested_refs: Senate Banking Committee hearings on Title I in New York City
sources: Themis Chronopoulos, Journal of Urban History, journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/1538513213487149

stops.name: Washington Square Park, Manhattan, the road under the arch
stops.date_confidence: attested that Moses proposed extending Fifth Avenue through Washington Square from 1952, that Shirley Hayes led the Save the Square campaign from that year with Jane Jacobs joining later, and that the park closed to traffic. FLAGGED: the research pool gave a 1958 Board of Estimate closure; the 1958 closure following the public hearing was a trial, and permanent closure to all vehicular traffic came in August 1959. Dated to 1952, the plan; month and day defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: He proposes to run Fifth Avenue on through Washington Square, under the arch and out the far side, as the spine of the Title I project rising to the south. Shirley Hayes starts a committee to save the square and works at it for six years; Jane Jacobs comes in later and brings the press with her. What is at issue is about four hundred feet of roadway, and a neighbourhood committee with a mailing list wins it off the Coordinator of Construction. The square closes to traffic on trial in 1958, and permanently in August 1959.
stops.quote: Critics are ex post facto prophets who can tell how everything should have been done at a time when they were in diapers, in rompers or Invisible.
stops.quote_source: Robert Moses, Comment on a New Yorker Profile and Biography (1974); verbatim as the Internet Archive transcription stands, capital I and all
suggested_refs: The Save the Square campaign papers; Washington Square Park chronology, washingtonsqpark.org/history
sources: New York Preservation Archive Project, Jane Jacobs record, nypap.org

stops.name: Lincoln Square, Upper West Side, sixteen hundred and forty-seven families
stops.date_confidence: attested; the Lincoln Square urban renewal, designated under the Mayor's Committee on Slum Clearance, cleared the racially mixed San Juan Hill district and displaced 1,647 families according to the redevelopment record, with construction running to 1962. Month and day defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: San Juan Hill is a Black and Puerto Rican district of tenements, churches and storefront businesses, and the Committee on Slum Clearance designates it. One thousand six hundred and forty-seven families are moved out. What rises on the cleared ground is Lincoln Center, a travertine campus for the opera, the philharmonic and the ballet, in use every night of the season since. Nineteen years later Moses answers the displacement figure in a pamphlet he pays to have typed and mailed. The relocation office rehoused a fraction of the families it moved out.
stops.quote: Ninety-eight percent of the ghetto folks we moved were given immeasurably better living places at unprecedented cost.
stops.quote_source: Robert Moses, Comment on a New Yorker Profile and Biography (1974)
suggested_refs: The Lincoln Square Title I redevelopment record and its relocation returns
sources: WQXR, 'Remembering the Ramifications of Robert Moses's Lincoln Square Renewal Project', wqxr.org

stops.name: Tavern on the Green, Central Park, the mothers and the bulldozers
stops.date_confidence: attested to April 1956 for the clearing and the litigation that halted it; the exact day is not established in the sources consulted and 24 April is used to order the segment. Pin inherited from the interlock pass for the Tavern on the Green site. The ground is inside the park Frederick Law Olmsted and Calvert Vaux laid out from 1858; the two existing journey files establish the design, not this episode.
stops.campa: The department starts felling trees in a wooded hollow off the West Drive to make a parking lot for the Tavern on the Green restaurant. Mothers from the buildings across the street, whose children play in that hollow, stand in front of the machines with their prams, and their lawyers get an injunction. The photographs run in every paper in the city: a line of prams, and behind them the machines standing idle. Moses gives way. He builds a playground on the spot instead, on ground Olmsted and Vaux drew as landscape, and the parking lot is never made.

stops.name: Atlantic and Flatbush Avenues, Brooklyn, the stadium he will not condemn for
stops.date_confidence: attested that Walter O'Malley sought condemnation under Title I for a privately financed domed stadium at Atlantic and Flatbush, that Moses refused and offered Flushing Meadows instead, and that the Dodgers left for Los Angeles after the 1957 season. FLAGGED: the research pool's coordinate plotted in Park Slope, matching neither the Ebbets Field site nor the Atlantic-Flatbush parcel; the pin here is the Atlantic-Flatbush parcel the claim describes. stops.campa: Walter O'Malley wants to build a domed stadium with his own money at Atlantic and Flatbush, over the Long Island Rail Road terminal, and he needs the city to condemn the land for him under Title I. Moses refuses. Title I is for slum clearance, not for a ball club, and he offers instead a city-owned stadium out at Flushing Meadows, which O'Malley will not take because there he would be a tenant. After the 1957 season the Dodgers go to Los Angeles. The city builds the Flushing Meadows stadium anyway, and in 1964 the Mets open it.

stops.name: Delacorte Theater, Central Park, the Shakespeare he tries to charge for
stops.date_confidence: attested; in 1959 a court found the Parks Department's attempt to charge admission for Joseph Papp's free Shakespeare productions arbitrary and capricious, and the dispute led to the building of the Delacorte Theater in 1962. Month and day of the ruling not established in the sources consulted, defaulted to June 1959.
stops.campa: Joseph Papp has been staging Shakespeare free on the grass, and Moses rules that the audiences are destroying the lawn and must pay admission to cover the reseeding. Papp will not charge the public. The department pulls his permit, Papp sues, and a court finds the department arbitrary and capricious. He has already lost it in the newspapers by then, weeks before the ruling. The city ends by building Papp a permanent open-air theatre near the Great Lawn, which opens in 1962.

stops.name: Albany, chairman of the Power Authority
stops.date_confidence: attested that Governor Thomas E. Dewey appointed Moses chairman of the Power Authority of the State of New York in 1954, and that from that post he drove the St. Lawrence and Niagara hydroelectric projects to completion. Month and day not established, defaulted to 01-01. Pin inherited from the interlock pass as the Albany Executive Chamber coordinate.
stops.campa: Governor Thomas E. Dewey makes him chairman of the Power Authority of the State of New York, and Moses acquires a fourth kind of money: the revenue of rivers. Two projects are waiting, each stalled for decades by treaty, litigation and Congress. The St. Lawrence power dam has to be built jointly with Ontario; the Niagara project waits on a federal licence New York has been refused since the 1920s. He is sixty-five years old and has never built a generator in his life. Within eight years both rivers are producing current.

stops.name: Tuscarora Reservation, near Lewiston, the taking
stops.date_confidence: attested; the Federal Power Commission's order of 5 May 1958 delineated the 1,383-acre reservoir area, used here as the anchor date, the Tuscarora filed in the D.C. Circuit on 16 May 1958, and Federal Power Commission v. Tuscarora Indian Nation was argued 7 December 1959 and decided 7 March 1960. FLAGGED: the research pool attached the acreage to a 28 March 1958 condemnation petition, which the court records do not support, and gave final-impact figures of about 550 acres and 37 homes that could not be verified and are omitted here.
stops.campa: The Niagara project needs a reservoir, and the Power Authority moves against 1,383 acres of the Tuscarora Reservation to get it. The Tuscarora will not sell. They block the surveyors on the ground and fight the taking through the federal courts to Washington. In 1960 the Supreme Court holds that the Federal Power Commission may license the taking on payment of just compensation, because the reservation is not a federal reservation within the meaning of the statute. The reservoir is built above Lewiston on land nobody sold.

stops.name: Moses-Saunders Power Dam, Massena, the Lost Villages
stops.date_confidence: attested; the first R.H. Saunders generating unit entered service in July 1958, and roughly 6,500 people in ten eastern Ontario communities were relocated ahead of the flooding that created Lake St. Lawrence. FLAGGED: the research pool's coordinate plotted about 1.2 km off, in the river channel; corrected here to the dam structure itself.
stops.campa: The dam closes the St. Lawrence between Massena and Cornwall, and behind it the river rises into Lake St. Lawrence. On the Canadian side ten communities go under the water. About six thousand five hundred people are moved out of what Ontario afterwards calls the Lost Villages: houses jacked up onto trailers and hauled to new townsites, cemeteries opened and reburied, roads ending at a shoreline that did not exist the year before. The first Saunders generating unit comes on line in July 1958.

stops.name: Robert Moses Niagara Power Plant, Lewiston, first power
stops.date_confidence: attested that first power flowed in 1961 from the accelerated Niagara project, undertaken after the Schoellkopf plant collapse of 7 June 1956, and that Moses resigned the Power Authority chairmanship in 1962 under Governor Nelson Rockefeller's consolidation of state boards. The 10 February 1961 date orders the segment; the precise day of first generation is not established in the sources consulted. FLAGGED: the pool's coordinate plotted about 2.9 km south of the plant, in the gorge below Lewiston; corrected here.
stops.campa: The Schoellkopf plant fell into the gorge in 1956 and took a third of western New York's electricity with it, and Congress finally licenses the state to build. Moses drives the replacement through in under three years: conduits buried for miles from above the falls, a powerhouse cut into the gorge wall at Lewiston, and one of the largest hydroelectric outputs in the world the day it starts. The state puts his name on it while he is alive to read the sign. He resigns the Power Authority chairmanship the following year, under Nelson Rockefeller's consolidation of the state boards.

stops.name: Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge, Bay Ridge, the approaches
stops.date_confidence: attested that construction of the Brooklyn approaches from 1959 displaced working-class Bay Ridge blocks, that the clearance decision belonged to Moses's programme, and that Othmar Ammann's organization designed the span, which opened in 1964. Month and day of the start of clearance not established, defaulted to August 1959.
stops.campa: Othmar Ammann designs the longest suspension span in the world, and Moses supplies the approaches, and the approaches run through Bay Ridge. Working-class blocks are condemned for the Brooklyn ramps. The residents hold meetings, picket the site, write to the mayor, and are moved out on schedule. The span belongs to Ammann's engineers and the clearance belongs to Moses's programme, which is not a distinction anyone carrying furniture down a stoop is obliged to make. The bridge opens in 1964, and Staten Island fills up behind it.

stops.name: City Hall, Manhattan, the offices given up
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1960 that Mayor Robert Wagner's ethics reorganization required Moses to relinquish the Parks Department, his City Planning Commission seat and the slum-clearance chairmanship on taking the presidency of the New York World's Fair 1964-1965 Corporation. The 23 May 1960 date orders the segment; the exact day is not established in the sources consulted.
stops.campa: Mayor Robert Wagner has been assembling an ethics reorganization, and the price of the World's Fair presidency is the city portfolio. Moses gives up the Parks Department after twenty-six years, his seat on the City Planning Commission, and the chairmanship of the Committee on Slum Clearance. He keeps Triborough, the state parks and the arterial programme, which is to say he keeps the money. Twenty-six years after La Guardia handed him the parks, the Parks Department belongs to somebody else. He is seventy-one.
stops.quote: I spent most of my principal in order to remain in public employment.
stops.quote_source: Robert Moses, Comment on a New Yorker Profile and Biography (1974)

stops.name: Fire Island, the hearing he walks out of
stops.date_confidence: attested that Moses walked out of a contentious 1962 hearing on extending a road along Fire Island after being compared to Hitler, and that the road was foreclosed by the creation of Fire Island National Seashore in 1964, campaigned for by the Fire Island Voters Association with attorney Irving Like and Interior Secretary Stewart Udall. Month and day of the hearing not established, defaulted to June 1962.
stops.campa: He wants a road down the length of Fire Island, a barrier beach of wooden walkways and summer shacks that has no roads at all, and the islanders organize against it behind a lawyer named Irving Like and eventually behind the Secretary of the Interior. At the hearing a speaker compares him to Hitler. Moses stands up and walks out of the room. Congress creates the Fire Island National Seashore in 1964, which forecloses the road for good, and the island keeps its boardwalks and its ferries.

stops.name: Unisphere, Flushing Meadows, the fair without the world
stops.date_confidence: attested; the fair opened 22 April 1964 and ran two seasons under Moses's presidency, and the Bureau International des Expositions refused recognition over scheduling rules, keeping the Soviet Union and many European states away. The Bureau International des Expositions has refused it recognition, because he insisted on two seasons and on charging exhibitors rent, so most of Europe and the Soviet Union stay away and six major nations exhibit officially. Attendance comes in at 51.6 million against a projection of seventy. The corporation runs a deficit, and when the gates close the promised park is again not finished.

stops.name: Randall's Island, Triborough folded into the MTA
stops.date_confidence: attested; the Triborough Bridge and Tunnel Authority was merged into the newly created Metropolitan Transportation Authority on 1 March 1968, ending Moses's independent control of the toll revenue after he resisted diverting surpluses to mass transit. FLAGGED: secondary sources that date the end of his TBTA chairmanship to 1981 are wrong, and the NYPL institutional record corrects them.
stops.campa: Governor Nelson Rockefeller creates the Metropolitan Transportation Authority and folds the Triborough Bridge and Tunnel Authority into it over Moses's resistance. The point of the merger is the toll surplus: thirty years of bridge money, which Moses has always spent on more bridges, will now go to subways and commuter rail. He is offered a consultancy and takes it, and the consultancy carries no powers of any kind. Forty-four years after the Long Island commission, he holds nothing he can spend. He is seventy-nine years old.
stops.quote: I never was in charge of mass transit.
stops.quote_source: Robert Moses, Comment on a New Yorker Profile and Biography (1974)

stops.name: 28 Thompson Avenue, Babylon, Mary Sims Moses dies
stops.date_confidence: attested; Mary Louise Sims Moses, married to Moses in 1915, bedridden with severe arthritis from about 1952, died at the Babylon house on 6 September 1966. Moses married Mary Alicia Grady, long his secretary, the following year. The Babylon house was the family's Long Island home from the 1920s.
stops.campa: Mary Sims Moses dies in the house on Thompson Avenue after some fourteen years bedridden with arthritis. They have been married fifty-one years. She kept this house through all of it, close to the commission headquarters and the beaches, while he worked seven days a week and dictated in the back of a car with the curtains drawn. Barbara and Jane are grown women. Within the year he marries Mary Alicia Grady, who has been his secretary for a quarter of a century, and leaves Long Island for an apartment in Manhattan.

stops.name: 1 Gracie Terrace, Manhattan, the forty-eight pages
stops.date_confidence: attested that Moses issued the rebuttal pamphlet Comment on a New Yorker Profile and Biography in 1974; the Internet Archive record gives 48 pages, photocopied typescript, no publisher stated, and supports the year only. FLAGGED: the research pool gave 23 pages and dated the book to 26 August 1974; The Power Broker was published 16 September 1974 by Knopf. The 26 August date is kept here for the pamphlet, which answers the July New Yorker profile and so plausibly precedes the book, but only the year is documented.
stops.campa: Caro's profile runs in the New Yorker across July, and Moses answers with a pamphlet he pays to have typed, photocopied and mailed to everyone he can think of. Forty-eight pages. He disputes the displacement figures, the chronology, his mother, his brother, his motives, and the competence of a man who has never built anything. The biography follows in September, twelve hundred pages of it. Frank Lloyd Wright had called him a night crawler years earlier, and he settles that account in the pamphlet too.
stops.quote: Frank's comparison of himself as a skylark and to me as a blind night crawler were of course just a quaint bit of Celtic humor.

stops.name: Robert Moses Playground, Manhattan, the park that carries the name
stops.date_confidence: attested; the naming resolution was introduced in the City Council in August 1981, weeks after Moses's death, Mayor Ed Koch signed the bill on 27 January 1982, and the park was dedicated on 28 March 1982 with a roller-skate parade setting off from Moses's former residence at 20 East 46th Street.

The resolution goes in that August, weeks after he dies, and Koch signs the bill in January. Of all the bridges and beaches and expressways, the thing in New York City that carries his name is a playground. The dedication is held on 28 March 1982, with a roller-skate parade setting off from the East Forty-Sixth Street building where the family lived when they first came down from New Haven.

stops.name: Randalls Island, the Triborough renamed for Robert F. Kennedy
stops.date_confidence: attested to 2008 for the renaming of the Triborough Bridge as the Robert F. Kennedy Bridge; month and day of the enacting legislation are not established in the sources consulted, defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: The state renames the Triborough Bridge for Robert F. Kennedy. It is the bridge Moses built first and held longest, the seat of the authority that made every later thing possible, the toll crossing whose surplus built the parkways, the beaches and the two other bridges of the same knot, and on the signs it now belongs to a senator shot in 1968, the year the authority was taken away from him. The tolls go where the 1968 merger sent them, into the subways and the commuter railways, which is the one use of his money he fought hardest to prevent. Drivers go on calling it the Triborough.

stops.name: Niagara Falls, the parkway unnamed
stops.date_confidence: attested to 2016 for the renaming of the Robert Moses State Parkway as the Niagara Scenic Parkway, amid a project to remove and reconfigure the roadway along the Niagara Gorge. Month and day not established, defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: The Robert Moses State Parkway along the gorge is renamed the Niagara Scenic Parkway, and sections of it are pulled up to give the rim of the gorge back to people on foot. The power plant a few miles downriver keeps his name and keeps generating, which is the arrangement the state settles on: the works stay, the name comes off the ones people have to look at. The parkway had held the city of Niagara Falls off its own waterfront for half a century. The state takes it out in pieces, one contract at a time, and the gorge rim comes back to walkers a mile at a time.
